text: A keypair file written by solana-keygen is a JSON array of exactly 64 byte values: the first 32 bytes are the Ed25519 secret seed and the last 32 bytes are the public key. Metaplex states the file 'must be a JSON array of 64 numbers'. (high confidence)

A Solana CLI keypair file is a JSON array of exactly 64 byte values: the first 32 are the Ed25519 secret seed and the last 32 are the public key. `solana-keygen new` writes it to ~/.config/solana/id.json unless --outfile is given (Agave builds home_dir/.config/solana/id.json). Metaplex states the file 'must be a JSON array of 64 numbers'. (high confidence)

A Solana keypair file is plaintext and the generation passphrase does not protect it. Anza's file-system wallet page says 'This file contains your unencrypted keypair', 'File system wallets are the least secure method of storing SOL tokens', and that even with a password 'that password applies to the recovery seed phrase, not the file'. Matt Mazur's walkthrough shows the CLI prompt itself saying the passphrase improves the seed phrase 'NOT the keypair file itself, which is stored as insecure plain text'. Anza's page gives no file-permission advice. (high confidence)
Metaplex advises separate keypairs per purpose ('Never use the same keypair for mainnet testing and production') so test scripts cannot send real SOL. (low confidence)

The Rust Signer trait separates infallible and fallible calls, and the infallible ones hide failure. pubkey() and sign_message() default to try_pubkey() / try_sign_message() with unwrap_or_default(), returning the all-zeros Pubkey or Signature when the signer cannot act. A local Keypair never fails (its try_sign_message always returns Ok and is_interactive is false), but remote or hardware signers report SignerError variants such as Connection, NoDeviceFound and UserCancel, so bot code that signs through a remote signer should call the try_* methods and check is_interactive. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Limit the blast radius of a file wallet. Metaplex's matrix pairs local testing with a no-passphrase file wallet, devnet/testnet with a file wallet and backed-up seed, small mainnet amounts with a passphrase-protected file wallet on an encrypted disk, and significant value with a hardware wallet or multisig; it also says never to reuse a keypair across mainnet testing and production. Anza likewise says large balances should not sit in a file system wallet. For a bot, that points to a dedicated hot key funded only with working capital (inference). (medium confidence)

Keypair files must stay out of git. Metaplex lists 'Never commit keypair files to git' and advises ignoring *.json. A CI secret scanner flags tracked files named id.json or *-keypair.json by filename alone, any JSON array of 64 integers 0-255, and base58 strings of about 86-90 characters. That scanner checks only the current tree, not history, so historical leaks need truffleHog or gitleaks, and exposed keys must be rotated rather than just deleted from git. (medium confidence)

The Rust read_keypair parser expects the text to start with '[' and end with ']' (otherwise 'Input must be a JSON array'), splits on commas, requires exactly 64 u8 elements, and then runs the same pubkey check. write_keypair emits '[' plus 64 decimal values separated by commas with no spaces plus ']'. Other tools must produce this same shape for solana CLI and Rust programs to read the file. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Keypair files are unencrypted. Matt Mazur notes the BIP39 passphrase protects the recovery seed phrase 'NOT the keypair file itself, which is stored as insecure plain text'. Metaplex's mitigation for a file-system wallet is chmod 600 on the file, and it recommends a hardware wallet or multisig for significant mainnet value. (medium confidence)

Anza's remediation guidance after the web3.js compromise: verify that no application was ever built or deployed with 1.95.6 or 1.95.7 as a direct or transitive dependency, and rotate any suspect authority keys, explicitly including multisigs, program authorities and server keypairs. A bot whose keypair file or env var was loaded by an affected build should be treated as compromised. (high confidence)

Nothing encrypts a keypair file. The CLI itself warns that the BIP39 passphrase 'improves security of the recovery seed phrase NOT the keypair file itself, which is stored as insecure plain text' (quoted by Matt Mazur). Anza's file-system-wallet page says the file holds 'your unencrypted keypair', that the password 'applies to the recovery seed phrase, not the file', that file system wallets are 'the least secure method of storing SOL tokens', and that 'Anyone with access to this file will have access to all tokens sent to its public key'. (high confidence)

Rust Keypair deliberately has no Clone: the doc comment calls a second in-memory copy of secret keys 'usually a bad idea' and points to insecure_clone for tests or std::sync::Arc<Keypair> otherwise. TryFrom<&[u8]> copies the seed into a Zeroizing buffer so the transient copy is wiped. Signer is implemented for any Deref container (Box, Rc, Arc, &), so one Arc<Keypair> can be shared across bot tasks without copying key bytes. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Anza's guidance after the web3.js compromise: verify that no application was ever built and deployed with 1.95.6 or 1.95.7 as a direct or transitive dependency, and rotate any suspect authority keys, 'including but not limited to multisigs, program authorities, and server keypairs'. The advisory also asks developers to upgrade to 1.95.8, including those pinned to latest. A bot whose key file or env var was loaded by an affected build should be treated as exposed and rotated. (high confidence)

OWASP and Docker both advise against passing secrets as environment variables. OWASP's Secrets Management Cheat Sheet lists mounted files, a secret-store fetch and environment variables as the three ways to inject a secret into a container, and says environment variables are 'generally accessible to all processes and may be included in logs or system dumps', so they are 'not recommended unless the other methods are not possible'. Docker Compose's secrets page says the same and mounts secrets as files at `/run/secrets/<secret_name>`, with per-service access and normal filesystem permissions. (high confidence)

The Solana Foundation's solana-keychain library (Rust, TypeScript, Python, Go) gives one signing interface over Memory, Vault, Privy, Turnkey, AWS KMS, Fireblocks, GCP KMS, Dfns, Para, CDP, Crossmint, Openfort, Utila and Fordefi backends, plus an opt-in, Rust-only Ledger backend. Its docs describe the Memory backend as 'Local keypairs, development, testing'. Kora, the Foundation's signer node, selects across a signer pool with `round_robin`, `random` or `weighted` strategies; its example config lists memory, Turnkey, Privy, Vault and Openfort signers, and its config code also defines AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Para, CDP and Dfns signer types. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)
